Why is Chick-fil-A closed on Sundays?
They don't brag.
But they close both as an observance of the Christian sabbath and to give employees a weekend day off with their families.
For anyone in food service, that's unusual enough to be a serious perk.
Usually your “weekend” is odd days in the middle of the week.
I've been with Chick-fil-A for eight years and never have I once heard anyone “brag" about being closed on Sunday.
Being closed on Sunday is a legacy from Truitt Cathy from when he opened his first restaurant, The Dwarf Grill.
So there isn't any bragging because it's just the way it has always been.
If you’re old enough, you will remember that once upon a time (1950–1970) virtually everything was closed on Sunday.
It was considered a day of rest; inspired by Christian principles.
The general thought was that if you really needed something you should get it on Saturday or be prepared to wait until Monday.
And employees appreciated the respite.
Somehow civilization survived.
And, if I’m honest, I don’t believe things are better today because retail is an everyday opportunity…Same holds true for all the hype about stores opening on Thanksgiving.

Chick-fil-A promotes its restaurants being closed on Sundays as a part of its corporate values and commitment to family and faith.
The founder, Truett Cathy, established this policy in 1946, believing that employees should have a day for rest and worship.
This decision aligns with his Christian beliefs and reflects a broader philosophy of prioritizing work-life balance.

By emphasizing this policy, Chick-fil-A differentiates itself from competitors and appeals to customers who appreciate the company's commitment to these values.
It also creates a sense of anticipation, as customers know they can only enjoy Chick-fil-A on six days of the week, which can enhance brand loyalty and interest.
Why does Chick-fil-A brag that its restaurants are closed on Sundays?
